subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
The clip of Hafsa forgetting her lines in the school play had been shared two thousand times by Thursday. In the corridor, students from other classes smirked. In the classroom, phones lit up as she walked in. Hafsa took her seat and stared at the desk, her eyes hot. She couldn't explain that nerves had taken her voice; who would listen?

By lunch she had stopped answering messages. She told the teacher she had a stomach ache and sat on the library floor between the shelves. Jasleen found her there. “I'm not going to say anything clever,” Jasleen said. “I just didn't want you alone.” Hafsa nodded. Later Jasleen walked her to the counsellor, who listened, said none of it was Hafsa's fault, and phoned her mother that same afternoon.

qa.q: How many times had the clip been shared by Thursday?
qa.a: The clip had been shared two thousand times by Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa stop answering messages by lunch?
qa.a: Hafsa felt exposed and ashamed and could not explain what had happened, so hiding felt safer.

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen make that helped Hafsa?
qa.a: Jasleen sat with Hafsa without offering advice and later walked Hafsa to the counsellor.

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been thinking on finding Hafsa on the library floor?
qa.a: Jasleen probably felt worried and protective, unsure what to say, and chose simply to stay.

grounding: A teenager is flooded with mocking messages after a mistake goes viral, feels exposed and ashamed, and is helped by a peer and the school counsellor.

passage:
Dear Sachin Sir,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud. Last Friday I mixed up the answer in the quiz, and a classmate filmed it. Now the clip is on the class group, and people from other sections send me laughing lines. I keep reading them at night. I don't want to go to school on Monday. I keep thinking everyone has seen it, and nobody would believe I just froze.

Please don't tell anyone. I feel so stupid.

Rajni

P.S. (5 p.m.) I sent this at seven this morning. At lunch you came to the library, sat down and told me none of this is my fault, and that the principal must know so it can be stopped. You also phoned my mother this afternoon, and the group has been told to delete the clip.

qa.q: At what time did Rajni send the email?
qa.a: Rajni sent the email at seven that morning.

qa.q: Why did Rajni ask Sachin Sir not to tell anyone?
qa.a: Rajni felt stupid and ashamed and feared more attention, even though the email itself was a request for help.

qa.q: What did Sachin Sir do the same day that helped Rajni?
qa.a: Sachin Sir came to the library, said none of it was Rajni's fault, informed the principal and phoned Rajni's mother.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sachin Sir to open an email like this at the start of the day?
qa.a: Sachin Sir probably felt concern and urgency, knowing a student was frightened to come to school and needed action that day.

grounding: A teenager flooded with mocking messages after a mistake goes viral feels ashamed and unable to explain, and writes to a trusted adult.
